Morphological and life-history data for five mouse lines

Source: R/data.R
ratones_morpho.Rd

Cranial measurements and individual information for mice from the long-term artificial selection experiment on body weight analyzed by Penna et al. (2017). Selection for body weight at 49 days of age was carried out downwards in the s and h lines and upwards in the sp and hp lines, alongside a randomly mated control line t; the s/sp lines were inbred by limiting population size and the h/hp lines by full-sib mating in the first generations.

Usage

ratones_morpho

Format

A data frame with 329 rows and 46 columns. Row names are the individual IDs (as.character(ID)).

.id

line label combining the selection direction and the line, e.g. "control.t";

ID

individual catalogue number;

SEX

sex, "F" or "M";

GER

generation of the long-term experiment;

LIN

experimental line: t (control), s and h (downward selection), sp and hp (upward selection);

MADRE

catalogue number of the dam;

PADRE

catalogue number of the sire;

AGE

age at sacrifice, in days;

P49

body weight at 49 days of age;

line

the line as a factor with levels t, h'}, \code{s', h and s;

selection

direction of selection: "control", "downwards" or "upwards";

IS_PM, IS_NSL, IS_PNS, PM_ZS, PM_ZI, PM_MT, NSL_NA, NSL_ZS, NSL_ZI, NA_BR, NA_PNS, BR_PT, BR_APET, PT_APET, PT_BA, PT_EAM, PT_ZYGO, PT_TSP, ZS_ZI, ZI_MT, ZI_ZYGO, ZI_TSP, MT_PNS, PNS_APET, APET_BA, APET_TS, BA_EAM, EAM_ZYGO, ZYGO_TSP, LD_AS, BR_LD, OPI_LD, PT_AS, JP_AS, BA_OPI

35 cranial Euclidean distances, named after the landmarks they span. They are on the measured scale; log() is the usual transformation before fitting.

Source

Penna et al. (2017), archived at Dryad under CC0 1.0 (doi:10.5061/dryad.5gr8r ) and distributed by the MIT-licensed companion package https://github.com/diogro/ratones.

Details

Every individual carries a full set of 35 cranial Euclidean distances, measured as the mean of two replicas, plus the catalogue numbers of its parents. The distances are moderately integrated: the first principal component of their correlation matrix explains about 40% of the variance and the mean pairwise correlation is 0.35, so the traits carry partly independent information and a handful of them is enough for a well-identified model.

Weak identification

This is a long-term artificial-selection experiment that happens to carry a pedigree, not a design built to estimate a genetic covariance matrix. The animal model fits, but 329 individuals from 58 sires identify a 35-trait \(\mathbf{G}\) only weakly: the split between the genetic and the environmental covariance is left largely to the priors, so a heritability read from lmm_animal on these traits depends on the prior as much as on the data, and can move by a factor of eight between defensible choices. Use it as the small worked example it is, and use opossum, which carries marker genotypes and a design that does identify \(\mathbf{G}\), for anything about genetic covariance.

References

Penna, A., Melo, D., Bernardi, S., Oyarzabal, M. I., & Marroig, G. (2017). The evolution of phenotypic integration: How directional selection reshapes covariation in mice. Evolution, 71(10), 2370-2380. doi:10.1111/evo.13304

See also

ratones_pedigree, animal_design, lm_phen_cov

Examples

data(ratones_morpho)
dim(ratones_morpho)
#> [1] 329  46
table(ratones_morpho$selection)
#> 
#>   control downwards   upwards 
#>        67       121       141 
traits <- names(ratones_morpho)[12:46]
pc1_variance_share(log(as.matrix(ratones_morpho[, traits])))
#> [1] 0.4063927
